blocks.text:
Design the system behind a trending list, the top K most frequent search terms, hashtags, or product views over the last hour, computed continuously from a massive, ongoing stream of events. This is a genuinely different problem from the other two systems in this category. The likes counting system tracked one known post's aggregate. The leaderboard tracked a known, bounded set of players with exact ranks. This problem does not even know in advance what the full set of distinct items is, it could be hundreds of millions of unique search terms ever typed, and keeping an exact counter for every single one of them would need an amount of memory that grows without bound as new, never-before-seen items keep showing up.

The idea that makes this tractable is accepting a small, mathematically bounded amount of counting error in exchange for memory usage that stays fixed no matter how many distinct items the stream has ever produced, using a structure called a Count-Min Sketch, paired with a small heap that tracks only the current best candidates rather than every item that has ever appeared.

blocks.text: The system should ingest a continuous, high-volume stream of item occurrence events. It should return the current top K items by frequency within a recent, rolling time window, such as the last hour, not an all-time total. It should support several independent trending streams at once, for example top search terms and top hashtags tracked completely separately. And it should tolerate a small, known amount of counting error in exchange for the memory savings that make the whole approach possible.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first is the one that shapes literally everything else in this design.

blocks.alt: Five qualities the system must satisfy: bounded memory, high ingestion throughput, bounded approximate error, freshness reflecting recent activity, and fast reads

blocks.text: Memory usage has to stay bounded and fixed regardless of how many distinct items the stream has ever seen, since the whole point of this system falls apart if memory grows with cardinality the way a naive per-item counter would. Ingestion throughput needs to handle millions of events a second summed across every item combined. A small, mathematically bounded overcounting error is acceptable, and is in fact the entire trade this design makes on purpose. Freshness matters because trending specifically means recent, an item that was hugely popular a week ago and has since gone quiet should not still be sitting at the top of the list. And reads need to stay fast, since checking the trending list happens far more often than any deep analysis of the underlying stream.

blocks.text: The universe of distinct items is assumed to be far too large to track an exact counter for every one, potentially hundreds of millions of unique terms accumulated over time. A small, bounded, tunable overcounting error is accepted in exchange for a fixed memory footprint, worked out with real numbers in section 6. Trending is modeled as a rolling window made of several smaller time buckets, each bucket being its own sketch, with old buckets dropped as they age out of the window. As a refinement covered in section 28, the underlying approximate structure is used to narrow down likely candidates, with an optional exact recount only for that short list, rather than trusting the raw estimate for the final displayed ranking.

blocks.text: Say the platform ingests a million events a second across every distinct item combined, and over time has seen several hundred million distinct search terms or hashtags. A Count-Min Sketch sized with a width of two thousand and a depth of seven needs only fourteen thousand counters total, a handful of kilobytes, and that size never changes no matter whether the stream has produced a hundred distinct items or a hundred million. Compare that to the naive alternative, one exact counter per distinct item in a hash map: even at a modest fifty bytes per entry, three hundred million distinct items would need on the order of fifteen gigabytes for a single time bucket alone, and a rolling window needs several such buckets kept simultaneously. That gap, kilobytes against tens of gigabytes, is the entire argument for this design.

blocks.text: Incoming events are partitioned across several ingestion workers, and each worker maintains its own independent, partial Count-Min Sketch for the current time bucket, with no coordination needed between workers while ingesting. Periodically, these partial sketches are merged together into one combined sketch per time bucket, a rolling window's current total is the sum of every still-active bucket's sketch, and buckets that have aged past the window are simply dropped. A small heap tracks the current best candidates for the top K list, refreshed from the combined window sketch, and reads are served from a cache of that heap's current contents rather than recomputing it on every single request.

blocks.text: Each item occurrence is hashed by several independent hash functions, one per row of the sketch, and the corresponding cell in each row is incremented. An item's estimated count is the minimum value across every cell it hit, not the average or the sum. That specific choice, taking the minimum, is the trick that makes this work: a hash collision can only ever inflate a cell's value, since an unrelated item might also hash into that same cell, but it can never deflate it, so the smallest of several independently-hashed cells is always the tightest safe upper bound on an item's true count.

blocks.alt: An item is hashed by several independent hash functions, each incrementing one cell in its own row; the estimated count is the minimum across all cells the item touched

blocks.text: Trending has to mean recent, so rather than one sketch accumulating forever, the stream is divided into small time buckets, one minute each for instance, each with its own sketch. The current rolling window's combined sketch is just the sum of every bucket still inside the window, and a bucket that ages past the window's edge is dropped entirely, taking its contribution with it, which is exactly what lets an item that was popular an hour ago naturally fall out of the trending list without anyone needing to explicitly decay or subtract anything.

blocks.text: There is deliberately no table modeling individual events or per-item exact counts, since that is precisely the unbounded-cardinality problem this design exists to avoid. TopKSnapshot exists only to periodically durably record what the top list looked like at a point in time, useful for later analysis, not for serving live queries.

blocks.text: This is the one system in this category with essentially no durable, per-entity data model at all, and that absence is itself the design decision. Storing an exact row per distinct item would recreate the unbounded memory growth problem this whole approach was built to avoid, so the live state is a small, fixed collection of sketches and a small heap, with only periodic, summarized snapshots ever touching durable storage.

blocks.text: The happy path is ordinary stream ingestion, cheap and constant-time per event no matter how the item universe grows. The workflow worth walking through in detail is what a single item's estimate actually looks like with real numbers. Say an item hashes into cells holding values 42, 45, and 43 across the sketch's three rows, after some unrelated collisions have also touched two of those cells. The estimate is the minimum of those three, 42, which is guaranteed to be at least as large as this item's true count and, with the sketch sized appropriately for the traffic volume, very unlikely to be inflated by more than a small, bounded amount above it.

blocks.alt: The one-sided error guarantee: the estimate is never below the true count, and can only overcount by a small amount bounded by the sketch dimensions

blocks.text: This is a genuinely different, and more precise, correctness guarantee than the loose "eventually consistent" language used for approximate counts elsewhere in this project. A Count-Min Sketch gives a specific, one-directional guarantee, an estimate is never too low, only possibly too high, and by how much is a function the sketch's designer directly controls by choosing its width and depth.

blocks.text: Because a sketch is just a fixed array of counters being summed together, losing one worker's recent, uncommitted contribution is a minor, bounded, self-correcting event, not the kind of cascading failure a crash in a strongly-consistent, single-primary system elsewhere in this category would represent.

import heapq
import random
from typing import Dict, List, Set


# A fixed-size, mergeable structure that estimates item frequencies
# using bounded memory regardless of how many distinct items appear.
class CountMinSketch:
    def __init__(self, width: int, depth: int, seed: int):
        self._width = width                        # number of columns per row
        self._depth = depth                            # number of independent hash rows
        self._table = [[0] * width for _ in range(depth)]   # the fixed-size counter grid itself
        rng = random.Random(seed)                            # fixed seed, so results are reproducible every run
        self._seeds = [rng.getrandbits(31) for _ in range(depth)]   # one hash seed per row

    # Increments one cell per row for this item, in constant time
    # regardless of how many distinct items the sketch has ever seen.
    def add(self, item: str) -> None:
        for row in range(self._depth):
            column = self._hash(item, row)   # which cell this row maps this item to
            self._table[row][column] += 1        # bump that cell

    # Returns the minimum value across every cell this item hashed to,
    # the tightest safe upper bound on its true count, since a collision
    # can only ever inflate a cell, never deflate one.
    def estimate(self, item: str) -> int:
        minimum = None                              # smallest cell value seen so far
        for row in range(self._depth):
            column = self._hash(item, row)             # which cell this row maps this item to
            value = self._table[row][column]
            minimum = value if minimum is None else min(minimum, value)   # keep the smallest across every row
        return minimum   # the tightest safe estimate

    # Merges another sketch of identical dimensions into this one by
    # summing corresponding cells, which is exactly what lets independent
    # ingestion workers each maintain their own partial sketch.
    def merge_from(self, other: "CountMinSketch") -> None:
        for row in range(self._depth):
            for column in range(self._width):
                self._table[row][column] += other._table[row][column]

    def _hash(self, item: str, row: int) -> int:
        hash_code = hash(item) ^ self._seeds[row]   # combine the item's hash with this row's own seed
        return hash_code % self._width                 # map into a valid column index


# Tracks the current best candidates for a top K list, backed by a
# Count-Min Sketch's estimates rather than exact per-item counters.
class TopKTracker:
    def __init__(self, sketch: CountMinSketch, k: int):
        self._sketch = sketch                   # the shared frequency estimator
        self._k = k                                # how many top items to track
        self._min_heap: List[List[int]] = []          # [estimatedCount, item] pairs, smallest on top
        self._tracked_items: Set[str] = set()            # which items are currently in the heap

    # Called whenever an item occurs, re-evaluating whether it now
    # belongs among the current top K candidates.
    def on_item_occurred(self, item: str) -> None:
        self._sketch.add(item)                       # record this occurrence in the shared sketch
        current_estimate = self._sketch.estimate(item)   # this item's updated estimate
        if item in self._tracked_items:
            self._refresh_heap()   # this item's position in the heap may have changed
            return
        if len(self._min_heap) < self._k:                                     # still room in the top K
            heapq.heappush(self._min_heap, [current_estimate, item])             # add it directly
            self._tracked_items.add(item)
        elif current_estimate > self._min_heap[0][0]:                          # beats the current weakest entry
            evicted = heapq.heapreplace(self._min_heap, [current_estimate, item])   # remove weakest, add new
            self._tracked_items.discard(evicted[1])
            self._tracked_items.add(item)

    def _refresh_heap(self) -> None:
        refreshed = [[self._sketch.estimate(item), item] for _, item in self._min_heap]   # re-read every item's current estimate
        heapq.heapify(refreshed)
        self._min_heap = refreshed   # rebuild it with fresh values

    def current_top_k(self) -> List["ItemEstimate"]:
        return [ItemEstimate(item, count) for count, item in self._min_heap]   # a snapshot of the current top K candidates


class ItemEstimate:
    def __init__(self, item: str, estimated_count: int):
        self.item = item                       # the item itself
        self.estimated_count = estimated_count     # its current estimated frequency


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sketch = CountMinSketch(200, 5, 42)   # small demo sketch, fixed seed for reproducibility
    tracker = TopKTracker(sketch, 3)          # track the top 3 items

    # A stream with clearly different true frequencies: apple most common, then
    # banana, then cherry, with a handful of rare, low-frequency filler items.
    true_frequencies = {
        "apple": 50,
        "banana": 30,
        "cherry": 20,
        "date": 5,
        "elderberry": 3,
        "fig": 2,
        "grape": 1,
    }

    for word, count in true_frequencies.items():
        for _ in range(count):
            tracker.on_item_occurred(word)   # feed this item's occurrences into the tracker

    print("Current top 3 estimated items:")
    top_k = sorted(tracker.current_top_k(), key=lambda e: e.estimated_count, reverse=True)   # print highest first
    for item in top_k:
        print(f"  {item.item} -> estimated {item.estimated_count}")

    print("True frequencies for comparison:")
    for word in ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"]:
        estimate = sketch.estimate(word)
        true_count = true_frequencies[word]
        never_undercounts = str(estimate >= true_count).lower()
        print(f"  {word}: true={true_count} estimate={estimate} (estimate never undercounts: {never_undercounts})")

    top_k_names = {item.item for item in top_k}
    contains_all = "apple" in top_k_names and "banana" in top_k_names and "cherry" in top_k_names
    print(f"Top 3 correctly contains apple, banana, and cherry: {str(contains_all).lower()}")

items: Architecture: partitioned ingestion into independent, mergeable partial sketches, combined into time-bucketed windows, feeding a small top-K heap served through a cache.
Capacity: a million events per second platform-wide, hundreds of millions of distinct items ever seen, a fourteen-thousand-counter sketch against a naive tens-of-gigabytes-per-bucket alternative.
The core data structure: a Count-Min Sketch, worked through with a real, hand-verified estimate example and a genuine, mergeable implementation.
Database: deliberately minimal, since avoiding a per-item durable row is the entire point of this design, with only periodic top-K snapshots ever persisted.
End-to-end workflows: event ingestion and a top-K query, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Trade-offs: exact per-item counting versus a Count-Min Sketch versus stream sampling, compared directly on memory, accuracy, and where each breaks down.

Consistency: a precise, one-directional guarantee, an estimate never undercounts and overcounts only by a bounded amount, a sharper claim than the general eventual consistency used elsewhere in this project.
